title: Al-Waqi'ah, whole
hookLine: the three groups and the signs (Surah 56)
tomorrow: where is God when you move far away from home?

cards: Class rank. Leaderboards. Who finished first.
Those races get posted. Al-Waqi'ah, the Event, names a different one.

When the Event comes, it says, "ye will be three kinds": those on the right, those on the left, and a third group, in Pickthall's words: "And the foremost in the race, the foremost in the race: Those are they who will be brought nigh."
The word comes twice, as if once weren't enough.

teach.b: So which race? Not grades, and not who was born first. In Arabic the foremost are as-sabiqun, those who got ahead, and elsewhere the Qur'an names the track: race one another in good works.
The prize isn't a ranking. It's nearness: brought nigh. The surah paints all three groups in quick strokes.

Those on the right sit in spreading shade, by flowing water, with fruit never out of reach. Those on the left are in scorching wind, under the shadow of black smoke. Then the surah does something unexpected.
After gardens and warnings, it turns to things in your hands. "Have ye observed the water which ye drink?" Did you bring it down from the cloud, it asks, or did We?
If We willed, We could make it bitter; why, then, not give thanks? The seed you sow: do you make it grow? The fire you strike: did you grow its tree?
Here's the thing to tell a friend: this surah about the end of the world makes its case with a glass of water, a seed and a spark. The race toward God, in al-Waqi'ah, isn't run somewhere far away.
It's run at the sink and the stove, by people who notice what they're holding and turn it into thanks.
Being foremost might start as small as that: being the first to notice.

how: Some Muslims make a habit of reading Surah al-Waqi'ah in the evening; it is recited in Arabic, and its questions about water, seed and fire are often used to teach gratitude.

o: the night the Qur'an first came down
the Event: the surah of the three groups
the Spoils: a surah on the battle of Badr

games.q: the race and the signs — tap the pairs.
p: who brought it down from the cloud?

s: al-Waqi'ah sorts people into three kinds
those on the right, those on the left, and the foremost (56:7–11).
the foremost are simply the people who came first in time
they're ahead in the race toward God: the ones brought near.
the surah's signs are all far away, in the sky
it points to water you drink, seed you sow and fire you strike.

games.q: your little brother cries because he came in last on field day. what could al-Waqi'ah give him?
o: nothing matters anyway, so winning and losing are the same.
next year he should train harder, because the foremost always win.
there's another race, toward good, and anyone can be foremost in it.
games.why: the surah's race isn't field day or class rank. its prize is nearness to God, and it's run with ordinary things noticed and turned into thanks.

practice: If there's water near you, hold the glass and look at it before you drink. Take one slow sip and notice everything: cold or warm, the weight of it, the way it goes down.
For the sit, let the surah's question stay with you: have you observed the water which you drink?

wordCard.voice: Al-Waqi'ah. The Event: surah 56, with its three kinds of people and its signs as close as a cup of water.

orig.note: Arabic: the Event, the happening that will surely come; surah 56's name.

carryVoice: Carry this: the foremost, a race toward nearness that can start at the sink. That's this evening's reading.

sources.q: And the foremost in the race, the foremost in the race: Those are they who will be brought nigh.
Have ye observed the water which ye drink?

sources.ref: Qur'an 56:8–9, 56:27–33, 56:41–43, 56:63–72 (right and left, shade, water and fruit, wind and smoke; seed, water, fire); 2:148 (race one another in good works)
